title: WPMS/339/2021 of PADMA NEGI Vs STATE OF UTTARKAHAND

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND
AT NAINITAL
Writ Petition (M/S) No. 511 of 2021
Jamuna Devi .......Petitioner
Vs.
State of Uttarakhand & others .....Respondents
With
Writ Petition (M/S) No. 339 of 2021
Padma Negi .......Petitioner
Vs.
State of Uttarakhand & others .....Respondents
With
Writ Petition (M/S) No. 324 of 2021
Leela Devi .......Petitioner
Vs.
State of Uttarakhand & others .....Respondents
With
Writ Petition (M/S) No. 325 of 2021
Aneeta Devi .......Petitioner
Vs.
State of Uttarakhand & others .....Respondents
With
Writ Petition (M/S) No. 338 of 2021
Leela Syatari .......Petitioner
Vs.
State of Uttarakhand & others .....Respondents
With
Writ Petition (M/S) No. 340 of 2021
Rama Bhandari .......Petitioner

2
Vs.
State of Uttarakhand & others .....Respondents
Mr. T.P. S. Takuli, Advocate, for the petitioners.
Mr. G.S. Negi, Additional CSC, for the State of Uttarakhand.
Mr. Rajesh Sharma, Central Government Standing Counsel with Mr. Manoj Kumar,
Central Government Standing Counsel, for the Union of India.
Mr. Gopal K. Verma, Standing Counsel, for the State of Uttar Pradesh.
Hon'ble Sharad Kumar Sharma, J (Oral)
These are the bunch of six writ petitions, which engages
a consideration of a common question of facts and law, and this Court
will not hesitate to record my anguish, that it is a very pathetic state of
affairs, where the recognized war widows, are forced, to have, to have
a recourse to the judicial proceedings by invoking Article 226 of the
Constitution of India, for the payment of ex gratia amount which was
otherwise payable to them, as it has been envisaged to be granted to
the war widows, in pursuance to the Government Order No.169/XVII-3/14-09(31)/2014, dated 05.03.2014.
2. What is peculiar in all these cases are, that the act of
gallantry of the deceased husband of each of the war widows, who
were the Army personnel, is a fact, which is admitted by the
respondents by pleadings and records, and they have further admitted
the fact that the late husbands of the petitioners, herein, had laid their
life for the country, and while serving for the country in an army
operation or because of curbing insurgency in State of Jammu &
Kashmir, and yet they have been deprived of with the benefits, which
otherwise State itself has recognized to be paid to them by the
Government Order No.169/XVII-3/14-09(31)/2014, dated 05.03.2014.
3. I am of the view, and quite logically too, that war widows
cannot be distinctly treated, particularly, when the benefits are to be
extended to them for the gallant services rendered by their late
husbands, to the Nation. The precise fact, which engages
consideration in each of the writ petitions are detailed hereunder.

3
"In WPMS No.511 of 2021, "Jamuna Devi Vs. State of
Uttarakhand & others"
1. The facts of the present writ petition, are that the late Mr.
Nayan Singh, who was then posted as a "Naib Subedar", having
an Army No.JC-137587P, was attached to the Kumaun
Regiment, and while carrying on an insurgency army operation
against the terrorist, called as "Blue Star Operation", which was
conducted on 07.06.1984, he was killed in an army action, and
later on he was declared as a "battle casualty". It is not only
that, it is rather the President of India, himself who had
recognized the gallantry act of the late husband of the
petitioner, and had posthumously awarded him "Saurya
Chakra" on 26.11.1985, and in relation thereto, the respondent
No.7, has issued a certificate to that effect.
2. Owing to the aforesaid backdrop, there cannot be any
controversy, doubt or the dispute of facts, that the late husband
of the petitioner died in, "an army operation" and was a "battle
casualty", and his services to the nation was recognized by none
other than, His Excellency the President of India. Hence, the
petitioner would be entitled for the grant of ex gratia payment,
which has been provided by the State Government, under the
terms of the Government Order dated 05.03.2014.
3. It is only that the issue about the applicability of the said
Government Order and exgratia benefits given therein by the
Government Order of 05.04.2014, in relation to those "war
widows". In relation to the "battle casualties", had come up for
consideration before this Court in a Writ Petition (M/S)
No.294 of 2015, "Manju Devi Vs. State & others", wherein,
the prospects pertaining to the payment of the ex gratia
payment to the war widows, was adjudicated by the Coordinate
Bench of this Court vide its judgment dated 23.02.2018, and
whereby, implications and the aspect of benefits of the
Government Order dated 05.03.2014, was taken into
consideration, and the enhanced ex gratia was directed to be
made payable to the war widows, and the wider principle which
was laid down by the said judgment and it was in the light of

4
the ratio laid down by the Hon'ble Apex Court, in the judgment
reported in AIR 1967, page 1301, "D. R. Nim Vs. Union of
India. The relevant paragraph Nos.3, 4 and 6 reads as under:-
"3. Sub-rule (1) clearly makes Rule 3 the Controlling
Rule for the purposes of assignment of the year of
allotment. The Rule then divides officers into two
categories: (1) an officer in the Indian Police Service at
the commencement of the Rules, and (2) an officer
appointed to the Indian Police Service after the
commencement of the Rules. We are concerned with
the second category as the appellant was appointed to
the Indian Police Service in 1955. The second category
is again divided into two sub-categories: (a) officer
appointed to the service as a result of a competitive
examination, and (b) officer appointed to the service by
promotion in accordance with Rule 9 of the
Recruitment Rules. As the appellant was appointed to
the Service by promotion, we are concerned with the
second sub-category. The formula adopted works out
as follows: first find out the year of allotment of the
junior-most among the officers recruited to the service
by competition, who officiated continuously in a senior
post from a date earlier than the date of
commencement of officiation of the appellant. We may
again mention that the appellant started officiating as
Superintendent of Police on June 25, 1947. But,
according to the first proviso, if the appellant started
officiating continuously in a senior post from a date
earlier than the date of any officer recruited by
competition his allotment had to be determined ad hoc
by the Central Government. According to the facts of
this case, the first proviso applies and not the test
provided in Rule 3(3)(b) of the Seniority Rules. The
second proviso limits the operation of the first proviso
by dividing the officiating period into two classes: first,
a period before the date of inclusion of an officer in the
Select List and, secondly, the period after that date.
The first period can only be counted if such period is
approved by the Central Government in consultation
with the Commission. The appellant's name was
included in the Select List of 1956. Therefore, in the
case of the appellant, the period prior to 1956 had to be
approved by the Central Government in consultation
with the Commission.
4. We may here notice Explanation 1 to Rule 3,
because the Government of India also say that the
appellant officiated continuously as a temporary or
local arrangement. We will deal with this aspect later,
but for the time being we assume that there is no force
in the Government of India's contention and the
Explanation does not apply to the facts of the present
case. Therefore, according to the Rule the Central

5
Government had to determine ad hoc the year of
allotment after approving or not approving the period
of officiation of the appellant before 1956. The
Government of India say that they determined this by
issuing the impugned order, the relevant part of which
reads as follows:
"The Government of India have now decided
with the concurrence of the Commission that the
State Civil Service Officers who were officiating
prior to 19th May, 1951, but have been appointed to
the Indian Administrative Service after that date
should for purposes of fixation of seniority, be
allowed the benefit of their continuous officiation in
senior posts with effect from the 19th May, 1951. The
same decision will also apply in the case of State
Police Officers promoted to the Indian Police Service
after 19th May, 1951."
6. It would be noticed that the date, May 19, 1951, to
begin with, had nothing to do with the finalisation of
the Gradation List of the Indian Police Service because
it was a date which had reference to the finalisation of
the Gradation List for the IAS. Further this date does
not seem to have much relevance to the question of
avoiding the anomalous position mentioned in para 9
of the affidavit, reproduced above. This date was
apparently chosen for the IAS because on this date the
Gradation List for all the earlier persons recruited to
the Service had been finalised and issued in a
somewhat stable stage. But why should this date be
applied to the Indian Police Service has not been
adequately explained. Mr B.R.L. Iyengar, the learned
counsel for the appellant, strongly urges that selection
of May 19, 1951, as a crucial date for classifying
people is arbitrary and irrational. We agree with him in
this respect. It further appears from the affidavit of Mr
D.K. Guha, Deputy Secretary to the Government of
India, Ministry of Home Affairs, dated December 9,
1966, that "the Government of India have recently
decided in consultation with the Ministry of Law that
the Ministry of Home Affairs Letter No. 2/32/51-AIS,
dated 25th August, 1955, will not be applicable to
those SCS/ SPS officers, who were appointed to
IAS/IPS prior to the promulgation of IAS/IPS
(Regulation of Seniority) Rules, 1954, and the date of
the issue of the above letter if their earlier continuous
officiation was approved by the Ministry of Home
Affairs and Union Public Service Commission". It
further appears that "in the case of Shri C.S. Prasad
also, an IPS officer of Bihar, a decision has been taken
to give the benefit of full continuous officiation in
senior posts and to revise his year of allotment
accordingly". But, it is stated that "as Shri Nim was
appointed to IPS on the 22nd October, 1955 i.e. after

6
the promulgation of IPS (Regulation of Seniority)
Rules, 1954, and after the issue of letter dated 25th
August 1955, his case does not fall even under this
category". The above statement of the case of the
Government further shows that the date, May 19, 1951,
was an artificial and arbitrary date having nothing to do
with the application of the first and the second proviso
to Rule 3(3). It appears to us that under the second
proviso to Rule 3(3) the period of officiation of a
particular officer has to be considered and approved or
disapproved by the Central Government in consultation
with the Commission considering all the relevant facts.
The Central Government cannot pick out a date from a
hat - and that is 5 what it seems to have done in this
case - and say that a period prior to that date would
not be deemed to be approved by the Central
Government within the second proviso."
4. In fact, it is not in controversy and rather admitted, that in
compliance of the said judgment, the Court in its paragraph
No.9, of the judgment, has recognized the gallantry act of the
martyrs, and has affirmed the principles; that the widows were
entitled, and would fall to be within the ambit of the
Government Order, whose husbands have died, even prior to
the issuance of the Government Order, and it is not only that
after rendering of the said judgment, the benefit arising out of
the Government Order dated 05.03.2014, has already been
extended to the petitioner, therein of those writ petition.
5. Subsequent thereto to the above adjudication, the issue once
again crept in for consideration in yet another writ petition
being Writ Petition (M/S) No.1182 of 2020, "Parwati Devi
Vs. State & others", wherein, the Coordinate Bench of this
Court, once again while considering the implications of the
Government Order dated 05.03.2014, had taken into
consideration that the earlier judgment, which was rendered by
the Coordinate Bench on 23.02.2018, as referred above, and
same later on has been affirmed by the Hon'ble Apex Court in
the SLP, which has been dismissed on 26.11.2018. The
controversy pertaining to the entitlement of the war widows of
the ex gratia payment, with retrospective effect has been laid to
rest. Hence, it would be inferred, that they fall to be within the
ambit and the zone of considerations of the Government Order

7
dated 05.03.2014. Relevant part of the judgment dated
23.02.2018 is extracted hereunder:-
"11. Though, there is no specific challenge to the cut-off
date, but since the Court is dealing with the case of a war
widow and to do the complete justice, the Court reads
down the G.O. dated 5.3.2014 and declares that the same
shall apply retrospectively covering the cases of all the
army widows/parents for ex gratia payment to 9 mitigate
the hardships faced by them. The case of petitioner be
considered within six weeks from today."
6. The relevant paragraph of the judgment dated
04.11.2020, which was rendered in WPMS No.1182 of 2020, is
extracted hereunder:-
"Learned counsel for the petitioner further submits
that the aforesaid judgment rendered by Co-ordinate
Bench was affirmed in Special Appeal by Division
Bench of this Court and S.L.P. filed against the said
judgment was also dismissed by Hon'ble Supreme Court
on 26.11.2018.
Learned counsel for the respondents also do not
dispute the submission made on behalf of the petitioner
that the question as to whether the Government Order
dated 05.03.2014 would apply prospectively or
retrospectively has already been decided by a Co-ordinate Bench of this Court.
Since the question, as to whether the Government
Order dated 05.03.2014 would apply only prospectively
or retrospectively has been decided by a Co-ordinate
Bench of this Court, therefore, the present writ petition is
also disposed of in terms of the aforesaid judgment
rendered in WPMS No. 294 of 2015 decided on
23.02.2018. The Competent Authority shall consider
petitioner's application for grant of benefit of
Government Order dated 05.03.2014 and take
appropriate decision, in accordance with law, within a
period of six weeks from the date of production of
certified copy of this order. The decision, so taken, shall
be communicated to the petitioner within one week
thereafter."
7. In view of the aforesaid reasons, I am of the view that once the
principles of an enforcement of the Government Order dated
05.03.2014, for providing an ex gratia payment to the war
widows with retrospective effect, as it has been reckoned by the
State, by the Government Order dated 05.03.2014, has been
judicially affirmed up to the Hon'ble Apex Court. The

8
petitioner would undoubtedly fall to be within the zone of
benefit of the said provisions, and the stand taken by the State
that later on the State has legislated the Uttarakhand Martyrs
Dependent Ex Gratia Act, 2020. It will have no relevance for
the reason being that the Act was legislated much thereafter.
Apart from the fact that, it is in contravention to their own
decision which was taken by the State, which was taken by the
Government Order dated 05.03.2014, rather the issuance of the
aforesaid Act No.05 of 2021, was deliberately intended to
override the affect of the judgment, which has been rendered
under the welfare subordinate legislation, to the war widows
and hence merely, because of the restrictions imposed by the
subsequent Act of 2021, this Court is of the opinion that the
petitioner cannot be deprived of with the benefits, because it
has already been settled by the Hon'ble Apex Court; that the
effect of the judgment, which has been affirmed up to the
Hon'ble Apex Court; cannot be overridden by any subsequent
legislation.
8. An identical issue also came up for consideration before the
Coordinate Bench of Punjab & Haryana High Court in a
judgment reported in (2012) 68 Punjab Law Reports 452
Krishna Devi vs. Union of India and others wherein the
aspect with regards to the entitlement of an ex-gratia payment
to the army personnel and their widows, who died on account
of an army operation and were held to be battle casualty, would
be entitled for the ex-gratia under the terms of Government
Order or instructions. The Court held, that in those cases where
the death of an Army person is caused because of the
deployment in an operational area or battle field and there the
army personnel meets with the sad demise, the family of the
deceased army or para military personnel will be entitled to get
an ex-gratia on the basis of the Government of India
instructions dated 26.09.1998, (as it was then involved in the
said case). In fact, if para 9 and 12 of the said judgment is taken
into consideration, which has been extracted hereunder:-

9
"9. This ex-gratia lump-sum compensation is to be paid
irrespective of the other benefits which the family of the
deceased army personnel would be entitled to. As per para-4 of
these instructions, the conditions and guidelines to be observed
governing the payment of ex-gratia lump-sum compensation
are indicated in the annexure attached thereto. As per the
annexure, the main condition to be satisfied for the payment
of ex-gratia lump-sum compensation is that the death of the
employee concerned should have occurred in the actual
performance of bona-fide official duties i.e. a casual
connection should be established between the occurrence of
death and government service. Clause 8 deals with cases to
be covered by clause (c) of para 1 of the main instruction.
According to this Ex Gratia compensation is generally to be
restricted only to these cases where death of the service
personnel is directly caused by actual field operations.
Illustrative examples of cases covered under the instructions
dated 22.09.1998 have been also attached with the letter. All
these deal with situations where death is as a result of an
accident while performing the duties which would reflect upon
the active performance of duties such as travelling to site of
actual action or field operations. None of these indicate that
mere deployment in operation area would itself entitle the
families of the deceased defence service personnel ex-gratia
compensation under the instructions dated 22.09.1998, nor does
it cover the situation where an army personnel is deputed in the
operational area but dies because of some disease as is the case
in hand where the husband of the petitioner died on 01.10.2000
due to acute circulatory failure, brain (cerebral) anoxia.
Although the disease and death were regarded as attributable to
military service while performing bona-fide military duties, for
which petitioner has been granted special family pension but
the claim of the petitioner is not covered by the instructions
issued by the Government of India.
12. The claim made by the petitioner under the instructions
dated 30.09.1999 (Annexure P-6) issued by the Government of
Haryana cannot be accepted in the light of the subsequent
clarification issued by the Government of Haryana dated
07.11.2001 (Annexure R-2), according to which, the benefit of
the instructions dated 30.09.1999 for benefit of the ex-gratia
grant to be released to the War Heroes only belonging to
Haryana who die a heroic death in or during operations and
to the disabled personnel belonging to Haryana (during the
period 1.4.1999 to 14.6.2001) depending upon the
percentage of permanent disability as assessed for life of the
individual by the concerned medical authorities irrespective
of the fact whether they are retained in service as welfare
measure or boarded out. This ex-gratia grant is only to be
granted to the casualities taking place in or during
operations in order to recognize the acts of bravery and
sacrifice of the War Heroes. It has further been clarified and
mentioned that any casualty taking place in operational area but
not in operations i.e. where actual battle has taken
place/fighting etc. is not covered under the ex-gratia grant

10
policy of the State Government. No other type of casualty
except battle casualities and battle accidents is covered under
the Policy dated 30.09.1999. The judgment relied upon by the
counsel for the petitioner in the case of Santosh (supra) has not
taken into consideration the clarification issued by the
Government of Haryana dated 07.11.2001 (Annexure R-2)
which, when read in consonance with the Policy Instructions
dated 30.09.1999, would highlight the intention with which the
said instructions were issued by the Government of Haryana.
The subject of the instructions dated 30.09.1999 (Annexure P-6), which reads "Ex-gratia and children education grants to the
families of Armed Forces Personnel killed/missing/prisoners of
war/disabled in kargil and other sectors" also indicates the same
as has been clarified by the Government of Haryana vide its
instructions dated 07.11.2001 (Annexure R-2). In view of the
above, finding no merit in the present writ petition, the same
stands dismissed".
9. It has been laid down that for the benefit of an ex-gratia
payment, it has to be extended when the fatal incident has occurred
resulting to the death of an employee i.e. the army personnel, herein in
a bonafide discharge of his official duties. It means, that there has had
to be a close connection between the discharge of official duties and
its cause, resulting to the death and hence, the payment of ex-gratia
compensation, would be restricted only to those casualties, which are
caused on account of an army operation, because the intention of the
legislature to grant the benefit to the ex-gratia is only for the purposes
to recognize the gallantry act of war heroes of our great Nation India,
who died in a heroic death in army operation, or have been disabled
on account of army operation. Hence, in the instant cases since
undisputedly all the soldiers of the respective petitioners, who are the
widows, who had died during the army operation, they will be
classified as to be a war casualties and thus would be entitled for the
ex-gratia payment based on the said principle. Particularly when these
aspects of death of the army personnels of the petitioner war widows,
are the battle casualty, has not been denied by the respondents in their
pleading in their counter affidavit.
10. A reference may be had to yet one another judgment and
more importantly, it deals with a prime issue, as it engages
consideration in these bunch of writ petitions rendered in a judgment

11
reported in (2018) 6 Supreme Court Cases 363, State of Karnataka
and others vs. Karnataka Pawn Brokers Association & others. A
reference of this judgment becomes necessary in the instant case, as it
has been argued by the Addl. C.S.C. that on account of a subsequent
legislation, which has been framed by the State Government
governing the terms and condition for the grant of the benefit to the
war widows or to the freedom fighters. What would be its impact,
when the benefit to the widows has already been extended under the
prevalent Government Orders, which were enforced at the relevant
point of time. The Hon'ble Apex Court in the aforesaid judgment
particularly in para 19, 20, 21, 22, 24 and 25, has held as under which
are extracted hereunder:-
"19. In Shri Prithvi Cotton Mills Ltd. and Anr. v. Broach
Borough Municipality and Ors., a Constitution Bench of this
Court, dealing with the question of validity of a validation Act
passed with a view to get over the judgment of this Court, held
that even it has competence, the Legislature cannot merely pass
a law that a decision of this Court shall not bind. This Court
held as follows:
4........Granted legislative competence, it is not sufficient
to declare merely that the decision of the Court shall not
bind for that is tantamount to reversing the decision in
exercise of judicial power which the Legislature does not
possess or exercise. A court's decision must always bind
unless the conditions on which it is based are so
fundamentally altered that the decision could not have
been given in the altered circumstances......."
20. In the matter of Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal,
In re a Constitution Bench of this Court after referring to a large
number of authorities held as follows:
76. The principle which emerges from these authorities is
that the legislature can change the basis on which a
decision is given by the Court and thus change the law in
general, which will affect a class of persons and events at
large. It cannot, however, set aside an individual decision
inter parties and affect their rights and liabilities alone.
Such an act on the part of the legislature amounts to
exercising the judicial power of the State and to
functioning as an appellate court or tribunal.
21. In S.R. Bhagwat and Ors. v. State of Mysore, a three-Judge Bench was dealing with a case where the Petitioners were
held entitled to certain promotions and service benefits from a
particular date. Even though these benefits were given to them
the State did not give them the monetary benefits and, in fact,

12
passed a law which had the effect of denying the monetary
benefits due to the Petitioners, in terms of the judgments earlier
passed in their favour. After dealing with the entire law on the
subject this Court held as follows:
12. It is now well settled by a catena of decisions of this
Court that a binding judicial pronouncement between the
parties cannot be made ineffective with the aid of any
legislative power by enacting a provision which in
substance overrules such judgment and is not in the realm
of a legislative enactment which displaces the basis or
foundation of the judgment and uniformly applies to a
class of persons concerned with the entire subject sought
to be covered by such an enactment having retrospective
effect.........
xxx xxx xxx
22. In State of Tamil Nadu v. State of Kerala and Anr., the
Constitution Bench of this Court again dealt with the question
as to whether the Legislature could set at naught the decision of
the superior courts. After referring to a large number of
judgments, this Court laid down the following principles:
(i) that the doctrine of separation of powers is an entrenched
principle in the Constitution of India even though there is no
specific provision in the Constitution;
(ii) Independence of Courts from Executive and Legislature is
fundamental to the Rule of law and one of the basic tenets of
the Indian Constitution;
(iii) the doctrine of separation of powers between the three
organs of the State - Legislature, Executive and the Judiciary is
a consequence of principles of equality enshrined in Article 14
of the Constitution of India. Consequently, a law can be set
aside on the ground that it breaches the doctrine of separation of
powers since that would amount to negation of equality Under
Article 14 of the Constitution of India;
(iv) the High Courts and the Supreme Court are empowered by
the Constitution of India to determine whether a law made by
the Parliament or State Legislature is void;
(v) the doctrine of separation of powers applies to the final
judgments of the courts. The Legislature cannot declare any
decision of a court of law to be void or of no effect. It can,
however, pass an amending Act to remedy the defects pointed
out by a court of law or on coming to know of it aliunde;
(vi) if the Legislature has the power and competence to make a
validating law it can make the law retrospective;
(vii) even where the law is enacted by the Legislature appears
within its competence but if in substance it is shown as an
attempt to interfere with the judicial process, such law can be

13
invalidated being in breach of the doctrine of separation of
powers.
24. On analysis of the aforesaid judgments it can be said that
the Legislature has the power to enact validating laws including
the power to amend laws with retrospective effect. However,
this can be done to remove causes of invalidity. When such a
law is passed the Legislature basically corrects the errors which
have been pointed out in a judicial pronouncement. Resultantly,
it amends the law, by removing the mistakes committed in the
earlier legislation, the effect of which is to remove the basis and
foundation of the judgment. If this is done, the same does not
amount to statutory overruling.
25. However, the Legislature cannot set at naught the
judgments which have been pronounced by amending the law
not for the purpose of making corrections or removing
anomalies but to bring in new provisions which did not exist
earlier. The Legislature may have the power to remove the basis
or foundation of the judicial pronouncement but the Legislature
cannot overturn or set aside the judgment, that too
retrospectively by introducing a new provision. The legislature
is bound by the mandamus issued by the Court. A judicial
pronouncement is always binding unless the very fundamentals
on which it is based are altered and the decision could not have
been given in the altered circumstances. The Legislature cannot,
by way of introducing an amendment, overturn a judicial
pronouncement and declare it to be wrong or a nullity. What the
Legislature can do is to amend the provisions of the statute to
remove the basis of the judgment."
11. There, it had held, that there cannot be any doubt that the
legislature has a power to enact as a status or validating act, but it has
observed that legislative powers to enact or validating a law, which is
inclusive of the amendments with retrospective effect, could only be
limited to remove the causes of invalidity, when such a law was
passed. In fact, it intended to postulate that though a legislature
basically does have power, but it can correct the errors, which were
pointed out in the judicial pronouncements. But limited to the
amended law by removing the mistakes committed in the earlier
legislation, it will not effect or will lead to remove the very basis of
the foundation of the judgment which had been rendered by the
constitutional courts. An identical view has been expressed in para
25, of the aforesaid judgment of Hon'ble Apex Court, (which has
already been extracted), that for the purposes of removing of an
anomaly in a law, already decided by way of a judgment made by the

14
courts, though the legislature does has a power to remove, the
anomalies, but it cannot remove the very basic foundation of the
judicial pronouncements and its welfare purpose and it cannot not
alter or set aside the judgment in the manner and that too with the
retrospective effect by introducing a new provision of law and held
that the executive, would be bound by the judicial pronouncements
even after revalidation or legislating a new Law, which has always a
binding effect until and unless the very fundamentals on which it was
based are altered.
12. An identical view about the impact of the subsequent
legislation over the judicial pronouncement already rendered by the
courts, was yet again considered by the Hon'ble Apex Court in a
judgment reported in, (1995) 6 Supreme Court Cases 242, State of
Orrisa vs. Gopal Chandra Raj and others, wherein, while
answering the questions as formulated while deciding the said dispute,
the Hon'ble Apex Court in its para 7 has held, that rather has laid
down the basic foundation of the principles and the entitlement of the
legislature of its power to validate an act by removing the infirmity
which has already been indicated by the judgment, but while doing so
the legislature, cannot merely set aside or annul or override a
judgment of the court. Para 7 is extracted hereunder:-
"7. It is an undisputed fact that respondent nos. 1 to 15 were
appointed as junior teachers on different dates subsequent to
June 1971 and their selection had been made by a Selection
Committee not appointed by the State Government but by the
Director of Health Service. The question that arises for
consideration is whether in view of the Validation Act of 1988
inter se seniority of such junior teachers is to be determined in
accordance with clause (ii) of Sub-rule (2) of Rule 8 of
Recruitment Rules 1979 or it is to be determined in accordance
with clause (iii) of the said Sub Rule. Further question that
arises for consideration is that whether there has been any
lacuna in the Validation Act? But so far as the second
question is concerned, it is too well settled that the
legislature have the powers to validate an Act by removing
the infirmity indicated in any judgment and that too also
retrospectively but they cannot merely set aside, annul or
override a judgment of the Court. The judgment of the Court
was merely to the effect that the Selection Committee not
having been appointed by the State Government as required
under the Rules, the process of Selection got vitiated. The

15
Validation Act has removed the lacuna by changing the
definition of the Selection Committee and consequently
validating the appointments made by such Committee during
the period in question. We see no infirmity with the aforesaid
Validation Act. The contention of Mr. Javali, learned senior
counsel, therefore, cannot be accepted."
13. The Hon'ble Allahabad High Court in yet another
judgment, on an issue about the revalidation of an act and its effect on
a prior decision already rendered by the courts on the basis of the law
prevalent, prior to its revalidation, was considered by the learned
Single Judge of Allahabad High Court in a judgment reported in
Allahabad Weekly Cases 1996 (Suppl.) 672 Bijendra Singh vs.
Regional Deputy Director of Education, Agra and others, wherein
the learned Single Judge of Allahabad High Court in para 17 has
observed which is extracted hereunder:-
"17. Now it is an established principle of law that there is no
restriction on the plenary Jurisdiction of legislation by the
Legislature within the field or subject. in exercise of such
plenary Jurisdiction, the Legislature can remove informing in
any law Indicated in any judgment. The Legislature has
absolute power to give effect to such enactment either
prospectively or retrospectively. However, by such enactment,
the Legislature cannot set aside, annul or override a judgment
of the Court. The cases which have since been decided by the
Courts cannot be wiped out by such enactment. But those cases
in respect whereof no decision has been given by any Court or
which has not reached finality and is still awaiting decision are
excepted and can very well be attracted within the purview of
such validation even retrospectively. Validating Acts, are
enacted in order to remove defects in the statute retrospectively
for the purpose of saving the actions taken under such defective
statutes when such defects are pointed out in some judgments.
Such legislation removes the infirmity without affecting the
judgment already delivered in a particular case which remains
binding between the parties inter se despite such legislation.
Such legislation, therefore, is not an encroachment on judicial
power."
14. I am, also of the view that though there is no restrictions
on the exercise of plenary jurisdiction of the legislation, to validate a
law or substitute a law, but the exercise of plenary jurisdiction, would
only be to eradicate the pre-existing anomalies pointed out by the
judgments, over an existing law, but however while doing so the
legislature cannot set aside or annul, or override a judgment of the

16
court. Since it has been decided under the then prevalent law which
was in force at the relevant point of time and the same re validation
cannot have a retrospective effect, particularly when under the
circumstances of the instant case where the effect of a new legislature
framed by the State, was enacted and intended to withdraw a benefit
of its own welfare scheme of ex-gratia, to be paid to the "widows of
the martyrs", who had admittedly and by way of an evidence, also
have been established to be the "war causalities", and who had died
during the course of "army operation", the details of which has been
respectively considered in relation to each of the writ petitions.
15. This philosophy of extension of benefit of ex-gratia
payment, apart from the fact that it is recognising the gallantry of the
soldiers, who died for the country and was providing a financial
assistance, which may also be a subsistence for the survivors of a
soldiers family, its effect cannot be taken away at a subsequent stage
particularly, when it goes with the intention and the purpose of the
constitution, which in its preamble has described our country as to be
a welfare State.
16. The very welfare concept would also simultaneously
attract the implications of Article 14 of the Constitution of India and
respondents authorities cannot be permitted to carve out a distinction,
in order to deprive the benefit of welfare scheme of the ex-gratia
payment to the war widows, whose husbands have died in an army
operation for the Nation, and were held to be better casualties and the
logic behind the aforesaid principle according to the opinion of this
Court, would be that all the war widows, whose husbands have died in
an army operation, who had already availed the benefit under the
exgratia scheme of the State, which is a welfare scheme, and are not
the petitioners herein, they cannot be put to a march ahead, to the
claim of the war widows petitioners' herein, as they would also be
equally, entitled for an equal treatment of benefit under the welfare
scheme of the State of 2014, which only apart from recognizing the
gallantry act, salutes to the martyrs, recognises their contribution for
safety of the country, who died for the country. Hence, the subsequent
legislature will not override the effect of beneficial legislation, office

17
memorandum or circulars issued by the State. A similar view as taken
by the Hon'ble Apex Court in a judgment reported in (1994) 6
Supreme Court Cases 77 Bhubaneshawar Singh and another vs.
Union of India and another, which had dealt with the principles of
an effect of a validating act and its retrospective operation though the
power of legislature has been upheld to be valid, to apply a law
retrospectively and remove the defects to bring out the changes in the
pre-existing law; but then in para 11 of the said judgment carves a
distinction, which is extracted hereunder:-
"11. From time to time controversy has arisen as to whether
the effect of judicial pronouncements of the High Court or the
Supreme Court can be wiped out by amending the legislation
with retrospective effect. Many such Amending Acts are
called Validating Acts, validating the action taken under the
particular enactments by removing the defect in the statute
retrospectively because of which the statute or the part of it had
been declared ultra vires. Such exercise has been held by this
Court as not to amount to encroachment on the judicial power
of the courts. The exercise of rendering ineffective the
judgments or orders of competent courts by changing the very
basis by legislation is a well-known device of validating
legislation. This Court has repeatedly pointed out that such
validating legislation which removes the cause of the invalidity
cannot be considered to be an encroachment on judicial power.
At the same time, any action in exercise of the power under any
enactment which has been declared to be invalid by a court
cannot be made valid by a Validating Act by merely saying so
unless the defect which has been pointed out by the court is
removed with retrospective effect. The validating legislation
must remove the cause of invalidity. Till such defect or the lack
of authority pointed out by the court under a statute is removed
by the subsequent enactment with retrospective effect, the
binding nature of the judgment of the court cannot be ignored."
17. The said judgment, has yet again dealt with the same
situation, that the defect which has been rectified by the legislature by
amending a law with the retrospective effect or by a validating act, the
beneficial legislation on the basis of which the benefit has already
been extended to some of the identically placed war widows, the right
which has accrued under the then law cannot be taken away by
amending the law, in relation to the remaining war widows who had
been deprived of the exgratia payment, like it has been extended to the
other war widows of martyrs.

18
18. On the other hand the counsel for the respondents had
placed reliance on a judgment rendered by Hon'ble Apex Court in a
Civil Appeal No.6689/6690 of 2019, "Manju Tiwari Vs. Union of
India & others", contending thereof that the benefit of the liberalized
family pension, instead of special family pension, which was an
issue engages consideration therein before the Delhi High Court, was
declined to be granted, holding thereof that the widows, therein would
not be entitled for an ex-gratia lump sum payment, for the reasons
being that factually the said case was based upon altogether a different
factual matrix, where the Hon'ble Apex Court while deprecating to
extend the benefit of ex-gratia payment was on the ground, that it was
a ultimately, held that it was a "physical casualty and not a battle
casualty", because there the army personnel who was said to have
met with the sad demise was not by an act of participating in an army
operation, but rather he died on account of a sudden heart stroke.
19. In that eventuality, I am of the opinion, that where the
scrutiny has been made by the Hon'ble Apex Court and thereby
consequently upholding the view taken by the Armed Forces Tribunal,
in the said case, it has held that since there factually the casualty, was
on account of a heart attack and not because of an army operation; it
was held and factually determined to be a physical casualty and not a
war casualty. Hence, I am of the opinion, that the principle laid down
therein by the Hon'ble Apex Court, on which the reliance has been
placed by the counsel for the respondents, apart from the fact that
though it may be slightly different, because it was determining the
claim of entitlement of liberalized family pension, as compared to the
special family pension, but particularly when it was in relation to a
physical casualty, where the denial has been made for the payment of
ex-gratia payment and not a battle casualty. A reference may be had to
para 4 and 5 of the said judgment, which is extracted hereunder:-
"4. The petitioner filed an application under Article 226 of the
Constitution before the High Court, making a grievance that the
Custodian had debited the expenses for raising the coal while
the Coking Coal Mine was under the management of the
Custodian but had not credited the price for the quantity of coal
raised, which was lying in stock on the date prior to the date the
said Coal Mine vested under the Central Government. The High

19
Court allowed the said application holding that the petitioner
was the owner of the said coal mine and was entitled to credit
for the stock of coal lying unsold as on 30-4-1972. A direction
was given that account be recast and payment be made to the
petitioner.
5. The Central Coal Fields Ltd., one of the respondents of that
application, filed an application under Article 136 of the
Constitution, before this Court. Leave to appeal was granted.
But ultimately the appeal was dismissed on 23-8- 1984. This
Court said: (SCC p. 433, para 11) "Admittedly the amount
claimed from the owner represents the cost of extraction of the
coal from the mine. The appellants had conceded before the
High Court and Mr Sinha appearing for them before us
accepted the position that if the extracted coal had been sold
before the appointed day, the owner would have been entitled to
the price. The mere fact that the extracted coal remained in
stock at the commencement of the appointed date can make no
difference to the position. The expenses were to be set off
against the sale price of the stock to be received at the time of
disposal. Therefore, the stock of coal had to be taken into
account for balancing the position. Reliance on the definition of
'mine' and Section 10 of the Nationalisation Act to counteract
this conclusion cannot avail the appellants. Indeed, the
submission advanced on behalf of the appellants is so much
opposed to common sense logic of the matter that in the
absence of a legislative mandate we have no hesitation in
rejecting it."
20. Since the said case was based upon altogether a different
fact where the death due to heart stroke, the same would not be
applicable in the present case, where the Late husbands of the
petitioners, had already being held to be a battle causality.
21. Besides this, since the benefit sought for by the petitioner
being under the welfare policy of State, provided to the war widows
by recognizing the gallantry act of their Late husbands, who had laid
their life for the country, under the welfare Scheme of the State, the
implications of the Act; which has been promulgated in 2021, will not
have a retrospective affect, at all to cloud the benefit of welfare
scheme already enforce, by judicial decision. Particularly when the
entitlement, which has accrued earlier.
(2) In Writ Petition (M/S) No. 339 of 2021, "Padma Negi Vs. State
of Uttarakhand & others"

20
Principally the legal issue which is involved in this writ petition
too, already engages the same set of facts and considerations of law,
where the petitioner of the present writ petition, who too is a "war
widow". Only, there is a slight factual difference in this writ petition,
to the extent that the petitioner's husband, Late Mr. Uttam Singh, had

"Rakshak" in Jammu & Kashmir on 30.01.1996. The petitioner has
come up with the case, in the writ petition, that her husband was

of an ex gratia payment, as contemplated under the Government
Order No.169/XVII-3/14-09(31)/2014, dated 05.03.2014. For the

In Writ Petition (M/S) No. 324 of 2021, "Leela Devi Vs. State of
Uttarakhand & others"
The only factual differences, in this writ petition are that in this
case, the petitioner of this petition, who too is a widow of the martyr

"Rakshak" which was carried against the terrorist, in (Jammu &
Kashmir) on 15.06.1999, and he too was also declared as a "battle
casualty", but despite of the principle being settled by this Court, in

Apex Court, she has not been given and paid with the ex gratia
payment, as it has been envisaged by the Government Order No.
169/XVII-3/14-09(31)/2014, dated 05.03.2014. Hence, for the reasons
which I have already dealt with, in the above paras, while dealing with

writ petition. This writ petition too would stand allowed under the

21
payment to the petitioner and in case of failure, the petitioner would
be entitled for the remittance of the interest payable on the ex gratia
payment at the normal present prevailing bank rate, till the amount is

In Writ Petition (M/S) No. 325 of 2021, "Aneeta Devi Vs. State of

The petitioner is a "war widow" of late Sri Jiwan Singh, he had

In Writ Petition (M/S) No. 338 of 2021, "Leela Syatari Vs. State of

with the 21 Kumaun Regiment. Since the status of the late husband of

23
for an interest at the present prevalent bank rate, apart from drawing

23. Hence, for the reasons recorded above, the writ petitions
